rows.claim: Alexander the Great consulted the Oracle of Amun at Siwa in 331 BC; temple at Aghurmi

Abu Simbel guide, each fact below. Ramesses II (r. 1279–1213 BC). Temples carved in a sandstone cliff on the west bank. Four seated statues about 20 m high, with figures of Nefertari, his mother and children at their feet. Greek mercenaries' graffiti, 6th c. BC. Great Temple dedicated to Amun-Ra and Ra-Horakhty, three halls about 56 m into the cliff, Osiride statues, Battle of Kadesh scenes. Sun reaches the sanctuary about 22 Feb and 22 Oct. Small Temple dedicated to Nefertari for the worship of Hathor, statues about 10.5 m. Rescue 1963–1968, funded by more than 50 countries, rebuilt about 60 m higher
Nubian Monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae: inscribed 1979, ten component parts, UNESCO International Campaign 1960–1980
Edfu: temple of Horus, begun under Ptolemy III in 237 BC, completed in 57 BC; its plan along one main axis is the classic example of an Egyptian temple
Kom Ombo: double temple of the Ptolemaic and Roman periods, dedicated to Sobek (crocodile god) and Horus (falcon-headed god)
Saqqara: Step Pyramid of Djoser, designed by Imhotep as a pyramid in six stages; the Memphis area (Saqqara, Abusir, Dahshur, Abu Rawash, Giza) designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1979
Wadi Al-Hitan: inscribed 2005; fossils of the earliest whales (Archaeoceti), the youngest in the last stages of losing their hind limbs
Siwa: near the Libyan frontier; about 200 springs; old walled settlements of Siwa and Aghurmi on rock outcrops; dates and olives; oracle temple of Amun consulted by Alexander, ruins at Aghurmi

Valley of the Kings: burial site of almost all kings of the 18th–20th dynasties (c. 1539–1075 BC), in the hills behind Deir el-Bahari; 62 known tombs; corridor, chambers and burial chamber; part of the Ancient Thebes World Heritage site (1979); Tutankhamun's tomb alone escaped pillage, treasures exhumed from 1922

Philae described by UNESCO as the final bastion of ancient Egyptian religion; the Aswan quarries and unfinished obelisk as the basis of knowledge of quarrying; Qubbet el-Hawa tombs of officials in charge of Nubian affairs; the Monastery of St Simeon one of the biggest in Egypt; Kalabsha, Beit el-Wali and Kiosk of Qertassi reassembled near the High Dam; Dakka, Maharraqa and Wadi es-Sebua, and Amada and Derr, rebuilt near their former sites

Grand Egyptian Museum: called the world's largest archaeological museum; collection from Predynastic to Greco-Roman times, gathered from institutions across Egypt incl. the Egyptian Museum; designed by Heneghan Peng (Dublin); triangle-patterned facade and sloping ceilings echoing the pyramids; translucent alabaster entrance facade, shaded atrium with a colossal statue of Ramesses II over 3,200 years old, grand staircase of statues of gods and royals, tall windows facing the pyramids

Giza: three 4th-dynasty pyramids for Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure; the Great Pyramid, oldest and largest, completed early 25th century BC; counted among the Seven Wonders, the only one still standing; entrance on the north face; descending passage to an unfinished subterranean chamber; ascending passage to the Queen's Chamber and the corbel-vaulted Grand Gallery (about 46 m); King's Chamber lined with granite, holding a sarcophagus; five compartments above it, likely to relieve pressure; robbed in antiquity
Great Sphinx dated by most scholars to the reign of Khafre

Giza (official, 2026-10-26 review): 4th Dynasty; Great Pyramid built for Khufu (c. 2589–2566 BC), the other two for Khafre and Menkaure, his son and grandson; Khufu's oldest and largest; original height 146.5 m; no taller building for about 3,800 years; the plateau (area) ticket does not cover the Great Pyramid, Khafre or Menkaure, each a separate ticket. Replaces "completed early 25th century BC" in `g-inside-pyramids`. Prices and hours on the page are not used

rows.claim: Khafre's pyramid complex (official, 2026-10-27): Khafre (c. 2558–2532 BC), Khefren to the Greeks, son of Khufu; second pyramid complex at Giza, on slightly higher ground so it appears as tall as his father's; 143.5 m; core of local limestone; top still keeps polished fine limestone casing quarried at Turah; mortuary and valley temples among the best preserved of the Old Kingdom; the Great Sphinx a unique feature of his complex, beside the valley temple. Menkaure's (official): Menkaure (c. 2532–2503 BC), Mykerinos, most likely Khafre's son; smallest of the three, original height 65 m, base less than a quarter of the others'; bottom quarter of the casing granite from Aswan, over 800 km away, the rest limestone; three smaller queens' pyramids beside it. Giza Plateau page: the area ticket does not cover the Great Pyramid, Khafre, Menkaure, the Tomb of Meresankh III or the Workers' Cemetery. Hours and prices not used

rows.claim: Ras Mohammed National Park: declared in 1983; coral reefs and other marine habitats are protected

Red Sea protected reefs (official, 2026-10-27): Ras Mohammed, South Sinai, declared 1983, 778.2 km², national park, at the meeting of the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba; eastern edge a rock wall with the gulf's coral reefs; mangrove channel about 250 m separating the Ras Mohammed peninsula from Al-Baira island; colourful fish, endangered sea turtles; reefs surround it on all its sea sides. Nabq, South Sinai, declared 1992, 518 km², sustainable-use protected area; coral reefs, dense mangrove forests, desert, mountain and valley ecosystems; an attraction for diving, safari and birdwatching. Abu Galum, South Sinai, declared 1992, 425.7 km², sustainable-use protected area; mountains close to the shore; coral reefs, seagrass, lagoons; underwater cave system to more than 100 m, unstable and extremely dangerous

Karnak: one of the largest temple complexes; great temple of Amun-Ra with the precincts of Mut and Montu; built over many centuries without a single plan; Great Hypostyle Hall between the 2nd and 3rd pylons, decorated under Seti I and Ramesses II, 12 central columns about 24 m, 134 columns in all; outer-wall reliefs of Seti I's victories and Ramesses II at Kadesh

Luxor Temple: dedicated to Amun, Mut and Khonsu; commissioned by Amenhotep III, completed under Tutankhamun and Horemheb, extended by Ramesses II (court, pylon, obelisks); colonnade of 14 columns about 16 m; avenue of sphinxes to Karnak
Great Sand Sea is a dune landscape reached from the Siwa area; the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities highlights sandboarding there
Siwa Protected Area: declared 2002; official description lists safari and desert tourism among the area's tourism activities

Deir el-Bahari: bay in the cliffs east of the Valley of the Kings; name "northern monastery" (7th-c. monastery); Hatshepsut's terraced temple c. 1470 BC, uncovered 1894–96, partly restored, famous use of its site; Mentuhotep II temple c. 1970 BC; Thutmose III temple found by the Polish mission that began restoring the third terrace in 1968
Colossi of Memnon: two quartzite statues of Amenhotep III that flanked his funerary temple's gateway, now in the fields; the name Memnon is later Greek

Ramesseum: funerary temple of Ramesses II, dedicated to Amun and the dead king; 17 m seated statue, only fragments left; about half preserved; reliefs of Kadesh, the Syrian wars and the Festival of Min; the colossus inspired Shelley's "Ozymandias" (1818)

Medinet Habu: mortuary temple of Ramesses III, dedicated to Amun; fortified enclosure with towers imitating Syrian migdol fortresses; scenes of wars against the Libyans, Nubians and Sea Peoples; royal palace by the forecourt; Coptic town Djeme inside the walls in the 1st millennium AD

Valley of the Queens: burials of queens and some royal children of the 19th–20th dynasties; more than 90 tombs (entrance passage, short halls, sarcophagus chamber); Nefertari, princes Khaemwaset and Amenherkhepeshef; World Heritage with Thebes, 1979
Deir el-Medina: settlement of the craftsmen who worked on the royal tombs; best-preserved of its type; thousands of papyri and ostraca on daily life; artisans' tombs and three temples for the workers

Saqqara: along the desert plateau between Abusir and Dahshur; Djoser, 2nd king of the 3rd dynasty, Imhotep's pyramid in six stages, complex where mud-brick/wood/reed forms were first built in limestone; Unas (end of the 5th dynasty) first with the Pyramid Texts, continued by the 6th dynasty; Old Kingdom mastabas with daily-life scenes; Apis bulls in underground galleries, the Serapeum; Memphis area World Heritage 1979

Dahshur: just south of Saqqara; Sneferu's two 4th-dynasty pyramids; Bent Pyramid started at 52°, top reduced to 43.5°, only Old Kingdom pyramid with two entrances; Red (North) Pyramid built at 43°, first true pyramid successfully completed

SS Thistlegorm: British cargo steamship built in Sunderland in 1940; sunk by German bombers on 6 Oct 1941 while anchored in the Red Sea; cargo of trucks, motorcycles, boots, rifles, aircraft parts; two deck locomotives thrown beside the wreck; found by Cousteau in the early 1950s; recreational diving from the 1990s as Sharm grew; near Ras Mohammed

Blue Hole: submarine sinkhole north of Dahab on the Gulf of Aqaba; coral and reef fish; the Arch tunnel; reputation for the most diver fatalities, mainly from attempts on the Arch; operators require technical qualifications for the Arch
Ras Mohammed: southern tip of Sinai between the Gulfs of Suez and Aqaba; 1983; Shark Reef and Yolanda Reef as dive hotspots

Saint Catherine Area: monastery at the foot of Mount Horeb/Jebel Musa where, the Old Testament records, Moses received the Tablets; sacred to Christianity, Islam and Judaism; founded in the 6th century, oldest Christian monastery still used for its original function; Path of Moses with the Gate of Stephen and the Gate of the Law; mosque and chapel on the summit

Saint Catherine's Monastery: Greek Orthodox; founded under Justinian I on the traditional site of the burning bush; original granite walls and church of the Virgin; Transfiguration mosaic; small mosque within the walls used by local Bedouin, who act as guards; icons before the 8th c.; manuscripts mainly Greek and Arabic, Codex Syriacus (c. 400); Codex Sinaiticus now in London; 1975 find of some 3,000 manuscripts incl. missing Sinaiticus parts; UNESCO 2002

Saint Catherine's Monastery (official, 2026-10-26 review): built on the order of Justinian I (527–565) in 548–565 AD; full name "Sacred Monastery of the God-Trodden Mount Sinai"; Saint Catherine of Alexandria martyred in the early 4th century, her body found by the monks on nearby Mount Saint Catherine in the 9th century; the Church of the Transfiguration contains nine smaller churches, one the Church of the Burning Bush; a Fatimid mosque from the 12th century; a library of about 6,000 manuscripts. Replaces "by tradition the monks built a small mosque" and "church of the Virgin Mary" in `g-sinai`. Opening hours on the page are not used

rows.claim: Kom Ombo Temple (official, 2026-10-27): name from Arabic *kum* 'mound' and 'Ombo' from ancient Egyptian *Nubt* 'the golden (city)'; dedicated to Sobek (crocodile god) and Har wer (Horus the Elder); earlier temple in the New Kingdom (c. 1550–1069 BC); present structure Graeco-Roman (332 BC–395 AD), earliest royal name Ptolemy VI Philometor (180–145 BC), most decoration Ptolemy XII Neos Dionysos (80–51 BC); two parallel axes through the columned halls to two sanctuaries, southern (right) Sobek's, northern (left) Harwer's; Sobek god of fertility, water, inundation, vegetation, with Hathor and Khonsu; Harwer adult Horus, son of Osiris and Isis, victor over Seth, with Ta-senet-nefret 'the Perfect Companion' and Pa-neb-tawy 'Lord of the Two Lands'; column capitals; calendars of festivals; 2nd-century AD scene believed to show surgical instruments; Sobek and Harwer on their sides at the centre of the back. Hours and ticket prices on the page not used

rows.claim: Philae (official, 2026-10-27): monuments mostly Ptolemaic (332–30 BC); temple of Isis, mother of Horus, begun by Ptolemy II Philadelphus (285–246 BC); mammisi scene of Isis suckling Horus in the marshes; one of the last temples active, until Justinian I (527–565 AD) ordered pagan temples closed; last dated hieroglyphic inscription carved by the priest Esmet-Akhom, 394 AD; temple converted into a church, many inscriptions deliberately destroyed; temple of Hathor by Ptolemy VI Philometor and Augustus (30 BC–14 AD); Kiosk of Trajan (98–117 AD), once fronting the complex, roof gone, emperor offering to Isis, Osiris and Horus; all relocated from Philae to Agilkia during the UNESCO Nubia campaign of the 1960s. UNESCO rows above: "final bastion", campaign 1960–1980, inscribed 1979. Hours and ticket prices not used

rows.claim: Karnak (official, 2026-10-27 review): *Ipet-Sut* 'The Most Select of Places'; east bank of Thebes; Great Temple of Amun, cult of Amun of Thebes, wealthy priesthood with political power; from Intef II (c. 2112–2063 BC) to the Ptolemaic period, Roman additions; nearly every New Kingdom king (c. 1550–1069 BC) left his mark; precincts of Amun (largest), Mut (south), Montu (north), Akhenaten's Aten temple (east); east–west axis and a north–south axis toward Luxor Temple, sphinx-lined processional way used in the Opet Festival; Great Hypostyle Hall 134 columns, 15 m, the central twelve 21 m; maybe begun by Amenhotep III, bulk and all decoration Sety I and Rameses II; Hatshepsut's obelisk almost 30 m, over 300 tons; Akh-menu of Thutmose III at the eastern end; temple of Khonsu and temple of Opet in the southwestern corner; sacred lake. **Replaces** Britannica's "central columns about 24 m" in `g-east-bank` (the Kadesh reliefs stay on the Britannica row). Hours and tickets not used

rows.claim: Valley of the Kings (official, 2026-10-27 review): rulers of the 18th–20th dynasties, New Kingdom c. 1550–1069 BC; some royal family members and a few high-ranking non-royals also buried; East and West Valleys, the west with only a handful of tombs; over sixty tombs plus twenty unfinished pits; west bank for the setting sun and rebirth; pyramid-shaped peak, sacred to Hathor 'Mistress of the West'; hidden tombs against robbers; first confirmed burial Thutmose I (c. 1504–1492 BC), third king of the 18th Dynasty; Ineni: "in privacy; none seeing, none hearing". **Replaces** Britannica's 1539–1075 BC and "62 known tombs" in `g-valley-kings`. Hours and tickets not used

rows.claim: Hatshepsut's temple: queen who became pharaoh, c. 1473–1458 BC; Deir al-Bahari, west bank of Luxor, directly across the Nile from Karnak; *Djeser-djeseru* "Holy of Holies", designed by Senenmut, chief steward of Amun; three levels, each with a colonnade at its far end; open court beyond the portico on the upper level, Osiride statues of Hatshepsut against its pillars; mortuary temple, also cults of Thutmose I, Hathor, Anubis; open-air altar of Ra-Horakhty; Amun's sanctuary cut into the rock on the central axis; reliefs of rituals, festivals, transport of obelisks to Karnak; middle portico: Punt expedition (left, Punt thought near modern Eritrea), divine birth and claim to the throne (right)

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Deir al-Bahari: three man-made terraces rising to the cliff; site sacred to Hathor, stelae show her as a cow emerging from the mountain; Valley of the Kings on the other side of the hills; Nebhepetre Mentuhotep (c. 2055–2004 BC) chose the site for his tomb and temple 600 years before Hatshepsut; statues of Amun, Mut and Khonsu crossed the Nile each year to visit the royal mortuary temples, Hatshepsut's one of the most important stops. Name, 1894–96 excavation and Polish restoration from 1968: Britannica row above

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Wadi Al-Hitan: Western Desert, Faiyum Governorate; inscribed 2005; fossils of the earliest, extinct suborder of whales, Archaeoceti; emergence of the whale from land animal to ocean-going mammal; most important site in the world for this stage; number, concentration and quality of fossils unique, as are their accessibility and setting in a protected landscape; youngest archaeocetes, in the last stages of losing their hind limbs; part of the Wadi El-Rayan Protected Area; footpaths guide visitors to key localities, vehicles kept out of the property

Wadi El-Rayan Protected Area (Fayoum): declared 1989; waterfalls formed by agricultural drainage water; Ain El-Rayan: moving dunes with four natural sulphur springs; Gebel El-Rayan: deep gorges, favourite panorama point; Wadi Al-Hitan in its northwest: fossils about 40 million years old of primitive whales, shark teeth, shells and other marine animals, an open-air museum, fossilised mangrove in soft rock; threatened slender-horned (white) and Dorcas gazelles, fennec and sand fox, rare migratory birds of prey. Distance from Cairo not used

Wadi El-Gemal – Hamata Protected Area: declared 2003; 7,636.7 km²; national park; south of the Red Sea governorate; about 60 km of coast, on average about 50 km into the Eastern Desert mountains and about 10 km into the sea; Wadi El-Gemal one of the largest and richest Eastern Desert valleys, rare and endangered species; Gebel Hamata one of the highest Eastern Desert mountains; some of Egypt's largest and most important mangroves, rare and very sensitive; some of Egypt's best pristine reefs, internationally famous, along the shore and as submerged islands; important seagrass meadows; islands of international importance for breeding birds and sea turtles; Egypt's most important sea turtle nesting beaches. Distance from Cairo not used

Hanging Church: built over the ruins of Old Cairo's Roman fort; three rows of marble columns, four wings; ceiling like Noah's Ark; 11th-c. marble pulpit on ten columns; icons from the 15th c. (oldest) and late 18th c.

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Ben Ezra Synagogue: oldest synagogue in Egypt, named after Abraham ibn Ezra, no longer in use; hekhal in Arabesque style inlaid with mother-of-pearl; geniza with documents over 850 years, found by Europeans in 1888, now in libraries worldwide

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Coptic Museum: largest museum of Coptic history, antiquities and art, about 16,000 artefacts; begun 1908 by Marcus Simaika Pasha on Coptic Church land, opened 1910, state property from 1931; within the walls of the Roman fortress of Babylon

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Abu Serga: church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, early 4th-century martyrs; crypt below the sanctuary, by tradition the cave where the Holy Family sheltered

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Luxor balloons: flights over the West Bank from sunrise; the Civil Aviation Authority and the Egyptian Airports Company paused commercial flights from 1 June to 30 August 2026 at the request of all operators, first time in 38 years, citing summer heat, described as annual; flights resumed in September; baskets in eight models for 2 to 32 passengers
Luxor balloons: on 13 March 2026 the Civil Aviation Authority cancelled West Bank flights after warnings of strong winds and unstable early-morning weather

2013 Luxor balloon crash: 26 Feb 2013, fire on landing, 19 of 21 on board died; Civil Aviation Authority report (7 Jan 2014) blamed a leak in an ageing fuel line; after a 2009 crash flights were grounded six months, pilot training increased and a designated launch site given

Egyptian Museum, Tahrir: opened 15 Nov 1902, architect Marcel Dourgnon; largest collection of Egyptian antiquities; highlights Narmer Palette, statues of Djoser, Khafre, Menkaure, Hatshepsut, Merneptah Stele, Akhenaten bust and Amarna collection, Yuya and Thuya on the upper floor since the 2018 reorganisation, treasures of Tanis; Tutankhamun's objects moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum; 22 royal mummies moved to the NMEC on 3 Apr 2021

National Museum of Egyptian Civilization: Fustat, Old Cairo, by Ain el-Sira lake; partly opened 2017, inaugurated 3 Apr 2021 with the Pharaohs' Golden Parade (22 mummies: 18 kings, 4 queens incl. Ramesses II and Hatshepsut, from the Egyptian Museum); about 50,000 artefacts, prehistory to modern; themes incl. the Nile, writing, state and society, beliefs; Royal Mummies hall; textile gallery about 600 pieces; nearest metro Mar Girgis, Line 1

Historic Cairo: World Heritage 1979; founded 969 as the Fatimid capital; gates Bab Zuwayla (south), Bab al-Futuh and Bab al-Nasr (north); Ayyubid Citadel as seat of government; Mamluk era 1250–1517 the largest, most complex Islamic city of its time; Ottomans kept and added; 19th-c. new Cairo left it intact; Al-Azhar a leading centre of learning since its foundation in 970; significant Fatimid mosques Al-Azhar, Al-Hakim, Al-Aqmar; Ibn Tulun (876–879) with spiral minaret and vast court

Al-Muizz Street: about 1 km from Bab al-Futuh to Bab Zuwayla; named after the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah; restored by the government from 1997; Qalawun complex 1285, al-Aqmar 1125, al-Hakim 1013, Bayt al-Suhaymi 1648–1796, Bayn al-Qasrayn, al-Ghuri complex 1505 south of Al-Azhar Street

Khan el-Khalili: first khan built 1382–1389 by Jaharkas al-Khalili, master of the stables of Sultan Barquq; the name now covers the whole market district between al-Muizz Street and the al-Hussein Mosque; El-Fishawy café established 1773
Sultan Hassan: mosque-madrasa built 1356–1363 under an-Nasir Hasan, Bahri Mamluk, near the Citadel; taught the four Sunni schools; Al-Rifa'i Mosque beside it, 1869–1912, neo-Mamluk

Cairo Citadel: begun by Saladin 1176–1183 on a promontory of the Mokattam hills; seat of government until Khedive Ismail moved to Abdeen Palace in 1874; dominates the skyline; Mosque of Muhammad Ali 1830–1848; Mosque of al-Nasir Muhammad 1318

Dendera: west bank of the Nile, Qena governorate; capital of the 6th nome; city of Hathor; temple one of the best preserved; Ptolemaic, completed under Tiberius, on foundations back to Khufu; hypostyle hall of 18 Hathor-headed columns, ceiling with astronomical scenes; roof chapels of Osiris where the zodiac (now in Paris) was found; small temple of Isis, sacred lake, two birth houses and a Christian church

Dendera zodiac removed in 1820 and replaced with a copy, original in the Louvre; twelve crypts with reliefs; relief of Cleopatra VII and Caesarion on the rear outer wall; mammisi of Nectanebo II and a Roman mammisi

Abydos: low desert west of the Nile near Al-Balyana; cemetery of the earliest kings (Umm al-Qa'ab); centre of the cult of Osiris, pilgrimage and burial near his tomb; temple of Seti I with seven sanctuaries through two hypostyle halls; King List of 76 predecessors from Menes; reliefs of particular delicacy; Osireion 8 m behind, underground hall with 10 pillars and a water channel, thought Seti's cenotaph
Temple of Seti I: continued by Ramesses II; part of the Osireion floods; the "helicopter" hieroglyphs are a Seti I inscription plastered over and re-carved under Ramesses II

El Gouna: Red Sea Governorate, 20 km north of Hurghada, 25 km from Hurghada International Airport; founded 1990 by Samih Sawiris, developed by Orascom Development; 20 islands surrounded by lagoons, 10 km of coastline; Downtown, Abu Tig Marina, Tamr Henna Square; water sports; El Gouna Film Festival since 2017
Abu Simbel sun alignment on or around 22 February and 22 October; temples relocated in the 1960s
Citadel of Qaitbay built 1477 on the site of the Pharos lighthouse, reusing its stone
Ras Mohammed declared Egypt's first national park in 1983
Abydos: the Temple of Seti I; Dendera: the temple built for the goddess Hathor (used in the `g-gems` guide)

rows.claim: Medinet Habu (official, 2026-10-27): mortuary temple of Ramesses III, architectural masterpiece for beauty and preservation; funeral rituals and worship of Amun; usual plan of the era, largely inspired by the Ramesseum; Ramesses III (c. 1184–1153 BC) most famous king of the 20th Dynasty, wars against Libyans and Sea Peoples, prosperity, victim of a royal harem conspiracy; mud-brick wall with two guard rooms; eastern High Gate (Gate of Ramesses III) between two towers with terraces, a similar western gate demolished; first pylon, first court, second pylon, second court, three columned halls, chapels, Holy of Holies, rooms behind; remains of royal palace, storehouses, administration buildings, royal stables; papyrus-capital columns and Osiride columns; temple of Hatshepsut and Thutmose III on a 12th Dynasty temple built on the tombs of Amun's ancestors; tombs of the Divine Wives of Amun-Ra (25th–26th Dynasties); canal to the Nile with a dock; enclosure used against Libyan attacks; reliefs of Libyan campaigns, Sea Peoples, hunting, expeditions, religious scenes and celebrations. Ancient Thebes inscribed by UNESCO 1979 (Ministry World Heritage page). Hours and ticket prices on the page not used

rows.claim: Qaitbay Citadel (official, 2026-10-27): one of the most important forts on the Mediterranean coast; built by the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Abu al-Nasr Qaitbay 882–884 AH / 1477–1479 AD over the ruins of Alexandria's Lighthouse; defence against naval attacks; limestone, about 17,550 m2; outer wall with defence towers; inner wall around the courtyard with rooms used as barracks and storage; main tower in the north-west, a massive three-floor square fort with half-circular corner towers carrying protruding balconies; water tank for soldiers and horses; enlarged and conserved in 2003. Visitor centre in a hall of the main tower with the French Center for Alexandrian Studies: nine bilingual panels (Royal Port, Timonium, Antirhodos, sea docks, shipyards, fortifications to Muhammad Ali), film on the Lighthouse site. Sunken site at the eastern tip of the Pharos peninsula, from the citadel's edge for 150 m, 6–8 m deep, work since 1994; Lighthouse debris (blocks over 20 tons in a line heading north); pieces from around Pompey's Pillar thrown in under Saladin in 1167 against a Crusader attack from Cyprus; over 3,000 architectural pieces, 36 shown at the Roman Theatre of Kom el-Dikka; three shipwrecks; 3rd century BC–7th century AD. Hours and ticket prices on the page not used

rows.claim: Mummification Museum, Luxor (official, 2026-10-27): in Luxor (ancient Thebes), explains the process of preserving the body; humans and many animals (cats, dogs, crocodiles) embalmed; Anubis (the jackal) god of embalming and mummification; process believed to take around 70 days with many rituals; organs removed through a small incision (10 cm) in the left side and preserved in canopic jars; body dried in natron from Wadi El Natron for about 40 days; wrapped in linen bandages; amulets within the wrappings; family placed the body in a coffin; displays tools, objects, equipment, ritual and religious significance; canopic jars, decorated coffins, mummified remains, amulets, statues of deities. Gallery: ankh amulet, mummified crocodile, statues of Anubis and Nephthys, mummy and coffin of Maseharti, ushabti figurines and painted chest, unguent jars, mummy of a fish (Lates niloticus). Policies: private photography permitted after paying ticket fees, no flash, no tripods; bags over 40x40 cm to the cloakroom. Hours and ticket prices on the page not used

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Alexandria National Museum (official, 2026-10-27): building originally a palace for Asaad Basili Pasha, one of Alexandria's wealthiest figures, Italianate style; acquired by the Supreme Council of Antiquities in 1996, converted into an archaeological museum, opened in 2003; collection of Egyptian arts and crafts from prehistory to the modern era; rare sunken antiquities from excavations in Abu Qir Bay; currency hall; Islamic-era weaponry; metals, ceramics, glass; gold, silver and jewellery of Muhammad Ali Pasha's family. Policies: photography with mobile phone free, no flash, no tripods; bags over 40x40 cm to the cloakroom; services: ramped entrance, elevator, parking, toilets, gift shop. Hours and ticket prices on the page not used

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Egypt itinerary planner (2026-10-28): a hub that only restates the 7, 10 and 14-day itineraries (lengths, Cairo/Luxor/Aswan core, transport options, cruise or hotels, sea or desert, what to leave out); no new facts

Luxor Temple (official, 2026-10-29): Ipet-resyt "Southern Sanctuary"; about 3 km south of Karnak, sphinx-lined processional way; oldest evidence 18th Dynasty (c. 1550–1295 BC); oriented towards Karnak for the Opet Festival (Amun, Mut, Khonsu visit Amenemopet); shrine of Hatshepsut (c. 1473–1458 BC); core by Amenhotep III (c. 1390–1352 BC) with columned hall, peristyle court and the Great Colonnade of two rows of seven columns; Divine Birth scenes (Amun-Ra disguised as Thutmose IV, c. 1400–1390 BC); colonnade decoration finished by Tutankhamun (c. 1336–1327 BC) and Horemheb (c. 1323–1295 BC); Ramesses II (c. 1279–1213 BC) peristyle court, pylon, colossi, two 25 m obelisks, one in the Place de la Concorde since 1836; Roman fort late 3rd century AD, sanctuary paintings of Diocletian (284–305) and three co-rulers, under restoration

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Egyptian Museum (official, 2026-10-29): oldest archaeological museum in the Middle East; Predynastic to Graeco-Roman; architect chosen by the first international competition in 1895, won by Marcel Dourgnon; opened 1902 by Khedive Abbas Helmy II; burials of Yuya and Thuya, Psusennes I and the treasures of Tanis, Narmer Palette, statues of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, papyri, sarcophagi, jewellery; mobile photography free, no flash, camera stand needs a ticket; bags over 40×40 cm, umbrellas, sharp items to cloakroom; no food except small water bottles; services incl. café, gift shop, elevator, library, ramp, Braille labels, parking, sign language, audio tour; ticket window closes an hour before closing; Ramadan hours

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Cairo Citadel (official, 2026-10-29): one of the most iconic monuments of Islamic Cairo, Muqattam Hills, panoramic view; ordered by Salah al-Din 572 AH/1176 AD, completed under al-Kamil ibn al-Adil 604 AH/1207 AD, official residence of Egypt's rulers until Khedive Ismail moved to Abdeen Palace in the mid-19th century; events to the end of the Muhammad Ali Dynasty (1952); Mosque of Muhammad Ali Pasha, mosque of al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, Ottoman Sulayman Pasha al-Khadim Mosque, Police Museum, Al-Jawhara Palace Museum, Military Museum; one area entry ticket and separate vehicle tickets

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Nubia Museum (official, 2026-10-29): born of the UNESCO Nubia salvage campaign (1960, at Egypt's request); work began early 1980s with a committee of the SCA, Egyptian universities and UNESCO; building by Dr. Mahmoud Al-Hakim, interior by Pedro Ramírez Vázquez; opened 1997; local sandstone and pink granite; Aga Khan Award 2001 (the Ministry writes "for Islamic Architecture"; the award's name is the Aga Khan Award for Architecture); three floors, main hall and diorama, lecture hall, library, education department, theatre, open amphitheatre; garden with part of a Fatimid cemetery, a cave with prehistoric rock inscriptions, a Nile waterway and channels, a reconstructed Nubian house; private photography after ticket, no flash; bags over 40×40 cm to cloakroom; evening hours Thursday–Friday; ticket window closes an hour before closing; Ramadan hours

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Museum of Islamic Art (official, 2026-10-29): one of the largest and most extensive collections of Islamic artefacts; idea 1880; opened 1903 under Khedive Abbas Helmy II; Mamluk-style façade next to the National Library; 2014 explosion targeting the Cairo Security Directorate opposite damaged the façade, restored and reopened 2017; two floors; astronomy, medicine, architecture; carved woodwork, ceramics, manuscripts; Mamluk key to the Ka'ba, textile with the oldest Kufic inscription; mobile photos free, no flash, tripods only for permitted commercial use; services incl. lecture room, library, elevator, Braille, accessible toilet, parking, ramp, gift shop, sign language

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Royal Jewelry Museum (official, 2026-10-29): royal family founded by Muhammad Ali Pasha 1805, ruled 150 years until 1952; palace built 1919 by Zaynab Fahmi in Zizinya; residence of Fatma al-Zahra', daughter of Prince Ali Haidar; European and Islamic styles, paintings, gilded ceilings, mosaics; two wings joined by a corridor, each with a basement and two floors; Muhammad Ali's diamond and emerald collar, gold chessboard, jewelled gold binoculars, gold cups, European jewellery sets of queens and princesses; no flash, tripods only for permitted commercial use; gift shop, café, parking

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Kalabsha (official, 2026-10-29): largest free-standing temple in Lower Nubia, well preserved; built under Augustus (30 BC–14 AD); Mandulis, also Isis and Osiris; pylon, forecourt, hypostyle hall, two transverse offering chambers, sanctuary; rock-cut chapel of Dedwen (south-west), small chapel probably of Ptolemy IX, 2nd century BC (north-east); Meroitic and Greek inscriptions, Graeco-Roman columns, crosses from use as a church; moved 1962–1963 from Kalabsha Island to New Kalabsha Island after the High Dam; Nubian monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae inscribed 1979

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Hurghada Museum (official, 2026-10-29): first antiquities museum in the Red Sea Governorate; first of its kind, a collaboration of the Ministry, the Governorate and the private sector, which funded the building; about 2,000 artefacts, Ancient Egyptian, Graeco-Roman, Jewish, Christian, Islamic and modern; theme of beauty in Egypt; morning and evening hours, ticket window closes an hour before each; Ramadan hours; no flash, tripods only for commercial use; elevator, gift shop, audio tour

links.name: Egypt, Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

rows.claim: Ras Mohammed (official, 2026-10-29): declared 1983; 778.2 km²; national park; 446 km from Cairo; meeting of the Gulfs of Suez and Aqaba; eastern edge a rock wall with the gulf's coral reefs; mangrove channel about 250 m between the Ras Mohammed peninsula and Al-Baira island; colourful fish, endangered sea turtles, rare marine life; reefs on all sea sides, a unique structure that shaped the area's natural life; earthquakes formed underwater caves beneath the island; Nubian ibex in the mountains, small mammals, reptiles and insects seen only at night, herons and gulls

Wadi El-Rayan (official, 2026-10-29): declared 1989; 1,757.9 km²; sustainable-use protected area; 150 km from Cairo; dunes, springs, wide water surfaces, plants, wildlife, marine fossils; lakes quiet and pollution-free; waterfalls from agricultural drainage, used for water sports; Ain El-Rayan: moving dunes, four sulphur springs, 16 desert plants, about 15 wild mammals, 16 reptiles, over 100 birds; Gebel El-Rayan: deep gorges, known as the split rock, panorama point; Wadi Al-Hitan in the northwest, about 40 million years; slender-horned and Dorcas gazelles, fennec, sand fox, red fox, wolf; peregrine, saker, osprey, ducks, quail, herons

Wadi Degla (official, 2026-10-29): declared 1999; 27.6 km²; natural monument; 10 km from Cairo; runs east to west about 30 km; Eocene marine limestone of the Eastern Desert, about 60 million years, rich in fossils; walls about 50 m; side valleys; rain falling from waterfalls shaped the "Degla Canyon", compared to the Grand Canyon; gazelles, ibex, hares, red fox, spiny mouse, bats; dragonflies, ladybirds, tiger moths, antlions; 18 reptiles

Petrified Forest, Maadi (official, 2026-10-29): declared 1989; 3.3 km²; natural monument; 30 km from Cairo; petrified stems and trunks in the Gebel El-Khashab formation of the Oligocene; layers of sand, gravel, clay and petrified wood 70–100 m thick; cylindrical rock pieces from centimetres to several metres; probably carried by an ancient branch of the Nile and petrified in place

Nabq (official, 2026-10-29): declared 1992; 518 km²; sustainable-use protected area; 500 km from Cairo; South Sinai; coral reefs, marine and land creatures, very dense mangrove forests, desert and mountain systems and valleys; gazelles, ibex, hyenas, reptiles, many migratory and resident birds, invertebrates; some Bedouin tribes live there; a draw for diving, safari and birdwatching

Abu Galum (official, 2026-10-29): declared 1992; 425.7 km²; sustainable-use protected area; 500 km from Cairo; South Sinai; mountains close to the shore; coral reefs, marine life, seagrass, lagoons, desert and mountain systems; animals, birds, wild plants; draw for diving, safari, bird and animal watching; about 165 plant species, 44 found only there; underwater cave system deeper than 100 m, unstable and extremely dangerous, must be protected

Lake Qarun (official, 2026-10-29): declared 1989; 1,298.3 km²; sustainable-use protected area; 90 km from Cairo; Fayoum; one of the oldest natural lakes in the world; remnant of ancient Lake Moeris; marine, river and continental fossil deposits about 40 million years old; huge river mouth; rhino-like "Fayoum animal", ancestors of elephants and hippopotamus, dolphins, sharks, ancestors of African birds; Aegyptopithecus, oldest ape, Oligocene; petrified trees; reptiles, amphibians, mammals; Roman and Pharaonic sites north of the lake; Qaret El-Rusas to the northeast; churches area and Deir Abu Lifa

Saint Catherine Protected Area (official, 2026-10-29): declared 1988; 4,412 km²; protected landscape; 500 km from Cairo; South Sinai; Egypt's highest peaks, from the great African rift about 24 million years ago that formed the Red Sea and Gulf of Aqaba; Catherine, Musa, Serbal, Umm Shomar, Al-Thabt; mountain views and oases around springs and wells unique in the world; Nubian ibex, Egyptian gazelle, hyrax, Sinai leopard, wolf, hyena, fox, hedgehog, spiny mouse, jerboa; 27 reptiles; 22 of the 28 plant species of Sinai described as unique in the world, medicinal and poisonous plants; churches and monasteries incl. St Catherine's, Byzantine, Pharaonic and later remains
